title: Cron Every Day at Midnight: 0 0 * * * and Other Daily Schedules
description: Use 0 0 * * * to run a cron job every day at midnight. Learn how it works, timezone pitfalls, and ready-made expressions for other daily schedules.

body.text: To run a cron job every day at midnight, use `0 0 * * *`. That means minute 0, hour 0, every day of the month, every month, every day of the week. If you want to check a variation before deploying it, the [Cron Expression Generator](/cron-generator) explains any 5-field expression in plain English and previews the next run times.
The midnight expression, field by field
Hours use a 24-hour clock, so midnight is hour `0`, not `12` and not `24`. A full crontab line looks like this:
0 0 * * * /usr/local/bin/backup.sh >> /var/log/backup.log 2>&1
Edit your crontab with `crontab -e`. The `>> ... 2>&1` part appends both stdout and stderr to a log file. Without it, cron tries to email the output to the local user, which usually goes nowhere.
The @daily and @midnight shortcuts
Many cron implementations (Vixie cron and its descendants) accept aliases. `@daily` and `@midnight` both mean `0 0 * * *`:

@daily /usr/local/bin/backup.sh
@midnight /usr/local/bin/backup.sh

These are not part of POSIX, so don't assume they work everywhere. Schedulers like GitHub Actions expect plain 5-field expressions. Check your platform's docs, or just use `0 0 * * *`, which works almost everywhere.
Common daily schedules
Only the minute and hour fields change for most daily jobs. Remember that minute comes first, which trips people up.

items: `0 6,18 * * *` — twice a day, at 6:00 AM and 6:00 PM
`0 */12 * * *` — every 12 hours, at midnight and noon
`0 0 1 * *` — midnight on the first day of every month

body.text: For jobs that run more often than daily, see [cron every 5 minutes](/blog/cron-every-5-minutes).
Pitfalls that cause real bugs
`* 0 * * *` is not midnight
Leaving the minute as `*` runs the job every minute of hour 0, which is 60 times between 12:00 and 12:59 AM. Always set the minute explicitly: `0 0 * * *`.
Cron uses the server's timezone
Standard cron runs in the system timezone of the machine (or the daemon's configured timezone). Many servers and containers are set to UTC, so "midnight" may be 7 or 8 PM in New York. Check with:

date
timedatectl

If you need midnight in a specific zone, either set the server timezone, or use your scheduler's timezone option if it has one. Some cron implementations support a `CRON_TZ=` line in the crontab, but this is not universal, so confirm it with your cron's man page.
Daylight saving time

In zones that change clocks, a job scheduled during the skipped or repeated hour can be skipped or run twice, depending on the implementation. Midnight is unaffected in zones that switch at 1 or 2 AM, but a `30 2 * * *` job commonly hits the spring-forward gap in the US. If a daily job must run exactly once, schedule it outside your region's DST transition hour or run the server in UTC.
Day-of-month and day-of-week are OR, not AND

If you restrict both fields, standard cron runs when either matches. `0 0 1 * 1` runs at midnight on the 1st of the month and also every Monday, not only on Mondays that fall on the 1st. For "first Monday" you need a guard in the script itself.
Percent signs in crontab lines
In a crontab, an unescaped `%` is treated as a newline. This breaks commands that use `date` formatting:

# Broken: everything after the first % is sent as stdin
0 0 * * * tar czf /backups/site-$(date +%F).tgz /var/www

# Fixed: escape the percent sign
0 0 * * * tar czf /backups/site-$(date +\%F).tgz /var/www
Everyone picks midnight
Lots of jobs on a shared machine, or lots of scheduled tasks hitting the same API, all fire at `0 0`. If exact midnight doesn't matter, offset it: `7 0 * * *` or `43 2 * * *` spreads the load.
Cron's environment is minimal
Cron jobs run with a stripped-down `PATH` and no shell profile. Use absolute paths to scripts and binaries, and set variables at the top of the crontab if needed:

PATH=/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin
0 0 * * * /usr/local/bin/node /srv/app/cleanup.js
6-field cron: Quartz, Spring and others
Some schedulers use a different format with a leading seconds field. Midnight there looks different:

# Spring @Scheduled (seconds minute hour day month weekday)
0 0 0 * * *

# Quartz (day-of-month or day-of-week must be ?)
0 0 0 * * ?

If you paste a 5-field expression into a 6-field scheduler, everything shifts one position and the job runs at the wrong time or fails to parse. Know which dialect your tool expects. The [Cron Expression Generator](/cron-generator) works with the standard 5-field format.
Test before you trust it

Before deploying, confirm the next few run times in the timezone your server actually uses. For `0 0 * * *`, consecutive runs should be 24 hours apart in local clock time, each at 00:00. The exception is a DST-observing zone, where the real elapsed time between two runs can be 23 or 25 hours around the transition dates. If you log timestamps from the job, you can convert raw epoch values with the [Unix Timestamp Converter](/timestamp-converter) to check what really ran.
FAQ
Is midnight 0 0 or 0 24 in cron?
It's `0 0`. The hour field accepts 0 through 23, so `24` is invalid. Midnight at the start of a day is hour 0.
How do I run a cron job at 11:59 PM every day?
Use `59 23 * * *`. That runs at the end of each day, one minute before midnight.
Why didn't my midnight cron job run?

The usual causes are a timezone mismatch (the server's midnight isn't yours), a relative path or missing environment variable in the command, an unescaped `%`, or a syntax error in the crontab. Redirect output to a log file and check `grep CRON /var/log/syslog` on Debian and Ubuntu, or `journalctl -u cron` on systems using journald.
What's the difference between @daily and @midnight?
Nothing. In implementations that support them, both are aliases for `0 0 * * *`.
